analysis.investment_thesis: Delhivery has the right story — India's e-commerce logistics buildout at 32.5% revenue CAGR — but at a P/E of 192x and operating margins of just 0.79%, investors are paying an extraordinary premium for a company that only just turned its first annual profit (INR 162 Cr in FY25). The PEG ratio of ~5.9x is more than five times my comfort threshold, and the 'hot logistics IPO' valuation profile is exactly what I've learned to avoid.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 32.5% over 6 years is genuinely impressive and reflects India's structural e-commerce tailwind — the market opportunity is real and large
Path to profitability is visible: OCF improved from -INR 634 Cr (FY20) to +INR 567 Cr (FY25), and operating income turned positive in FY24-25
Strong institutional backing (FII 48.57%, DII 34.98%) and clean-ish balance sheet with D/E of just 0.17
key_risks: P/E of 192x and forward P/E of 55.38x — even the forward multiple implies paying 55x for a business with 0.79% operating margins
Operating margin of 0.79% is perilously thin in a capital-intensive, competitive logistics market — any pricing pressure from rivals erases all profit
OCF was positive in only 3 of last 5 years; free cash flow barely positive at INR 92 Cr in FY25 despite INR 8,932 Cr revenue
red_flags: EV/EBITDA of -767.8 (negative EBITDA for most of its life) — the company's valuation has been entirely faith-based, not earnings-based
No promoter ownership whatsoever — the business is entirely held by institutional investors with no founding-team skin in the game, creating a different incentive structure
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Delhivery is the kind of company that gets Lynch excited on the business side — logistics backbone of India's e-commerce boom, genuine network effects, scaling revenue — but makes him wince on valuation. A first-year profit of INR 162 Cr valued at INR 34,676 Cr is a P/E of 192x. For that to work, you need earnings to grow 15-20x from here. That's possible, but you need operating margins to expand dramatically from 0.79% — and in logistics, with players like Blue Dart, XpressBees, and Ecom Express competing on price, margin expansion is far from guaranteed.

Lynch's key test for any stock: 'If I didn't own it, would I buy it today at this price?' The answer here is no. The story is right — India's logistics sector will be enormous — but I'd rather wait until operating margins cross 5%+ and the P/E compresses below 40x. Until then, this is a great business at the wrong price.
